claim: Recent studies have suggested close functional links between overt visual attention and decision making.
source: Recent studies have suggested close functional links between overt visual attention and decision making.
evidence: This is a general statement about existing literature, supported by the context of the manuscript and citations throughout the introduction.

claim: The frontal eye field (FEF) is a brain region crucial for guiding visual attention.
source: This suggests that the corresponding mechanisms may interface in brain regions known to be crucial for guiding visual attention – such as the frontal eye field (FEF).
evidence: This is supported by established scientific knowledge about FEF function and citations in the manuscript.

claim: Inhibitory transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) over the right FEF has a causal impact on decision making.
source: We show that inhibitory transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) over the right FEF has a causal impact on decision making, reducing the effect of gaze dwell time on choice while also increasing reaction times.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data from the TMS intervention and behavioral measurements.

claim: Inhibitory TMS over the right FEF reduces the effect of gaze dwell time on choice.
source: We show that inhibitory transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) over the right FEF has a causal impact on decision making, reducing the effect of gaze dwell time on choice while also increasing reaction times.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the choice task and gaze tracking measurements.

claim: Inhibitory TMS over the right FEF increases reaction times.
source: We show that inhibitory transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) over the right FEF has a causal impact on decision making, reducing the effect of gaze dwell time on choice while also increasing reaction times.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from reaction time measurements in the choice task.

claim: FEF inhibition reduces the relative discounting of the non-fixated option in the comparison process.
source: We computationally characterize this putative mechanism by using the attentional drift diffusion model (aDDM), which reveals that FEF inhibition reduces the relative discounting of the non-fixated option in the comparison process.
evidence: This is supported by computational modeling results using the aDDM framework applied to the experimental data.

claim: The decision process consists of sequential sampling of information, with choice implemented once enough net evidence is accumulated in favor of one option.
source: A prominent view in decision neuroscience is that the decision process consists of sequential sampling of information, with the choice implemented once the decision maker accumulates enough net evidence in favor of one of the options (Ratcliff et al., 2016; Shadlen and Shohamy, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature in decision neuroscience.

claim: Evidence accumulation is a domain-general mechanism underlying both perceptual decisions and value-based decisions.
source: Furthermore, experimental and theoretical accounts support the idea that such evidence accumulation is a domain-general mechanism underlying judgments about both the objective state of the physical world (perceptual decisions) (Bogacz et al., 2010; Forstmann et al., 2016; Gold and Heekeren, 2014; Hanks and Summerfield, 2017; O'Connell et al., 2018) and the subjective reward value of different choice options (Basten et al., 2010; Bhatia, 2013; Clithero, 2018; De Martino et al., 2013; Diederich, 2003; Fudenberg et al., 2018; Gluth et al., 2012; Hare et al., 2011; Hayden et al., 2011; Hunt et al., 2012; Hutcherson et al., 2015; Krajbich et al., 2015; Mormann et al., 2010; Philiastides and Ratcliff, 2013; Polanía et al., 2014; Rodriguez et al., 2014; Roe et al., 2001; Tajima et al., 2016; Trueblood et al., 2014; Webb, 2019; Woodford, 2014; Zhao et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by extensive citations to experimental and theoretical literature.

claim: Visual attention allows selective processing of information in the environment, allocating greater computational resources to elements of interest at the cost of diminishing processing of unattended components.
source: Visual attention allows us to selectively process the information in our environment, allocating greater computational resources to elements of interest in the visual scene, at the cost of diminishing the processing of unattended components (Carrasco, 2011; Chelazzi et al., 2011; Failing and Theeuwes, 2018; Itti and Koch, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature on visual attention.

claim: Sequential orienting of attention toward different stimuli is crucial for understanding the whole visual scene and guiding gaze through it.
source: Thus, the sequential orienting of attention toward different stimuli is crucial for understanding the whole visual scene and guiding our gaze through it (Eimer, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to established literature on attention and gaze.

claim: The effects of overt attention (by eye fixation) and covert attention (during constant fixation) on neural processing and underlying causal mechanisms are thought to be strongly related.
source: Attention can either be directed overtly (i.e., by eye fixation) or covertly (during constant fixation), but the effects on neural processing and the underlying causal mechanisms are thought to be strongly related (Moore and Zirnsak, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to literature on attention mechanisms.

claim: During decision making, subjects shift their gaze between options until one is selected.
source: Investigations into the link between overt attention and decision making have shown that, during decision making, subjects shift their gaze between the options until one of them is selected.
evidence: This is supported by citations to empirical studies on gaze and decision making.

claim: Overt attention may influence the evidence comparison process that guides choice behavior.
source: These findings have led to proposals that overt attention may influence the evidence comparison process that guides choice behavior (Amasino et al., 2019; Ashby et al., 2016; Cavanagh et al., 2014; Folke et al., 2016; Hunt et al., 2018; Krajbich et al., 2010; Shimojo et al., 2003; Towal et al., 2013; Glickman et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies proposing this mechanism.

claim: The attentional drift diffusion model (aDDM) formalizes the mechanism by which overt attention influences choice.
source: This proposed mechanism has been formalized by the attentional drift diffusion model (aDDM; Fisher, 2017; Konovalov and Krajbich, 2016; Krajbich and Rangel, 2011; Krajbich et al., 2010; Krajbich, 2019; Smith and Krajbich, 2019; Tavares et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by citations to the aDDM literature.

claim: There are reliable correlations between gaze patterns and choice.
source: and is supported by several reports of reliable correlations between gaze patterns and choice (Kovach et al., 2014; Sepulveda et al., 2020; Smith and Krajbich, 2018; Stewart et al., 2015; Vaidya and Fellows, 2015)
evidence: This is supported by citations to empirical studies showing correlations.

claim: Experimental manipulations of attention affect choice.
source: as well as experimental manipulations of attention that affect choice (Armel et al., 2008; Colas and Lu, 2017; Gwinn et al., 2019; Lim et al., 2011; Milosavljevic et al., 2012; Pärnamets et al., 2015), but see Ghaffari and Fiedler, 2018; Newell and Le Pelley, 2018.
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies, with some contradictory evidence also cited.

claim: Most existing studies have manipulated attention by means of salient stimulus changes or direct experimental instruction, which may possibly induce experimenter demand effects on choice.
source: However, most of the existing studies have manipulated attention by means of salient stimulus changes or direct experimental instruction, which may possibly induce experimenter demand effects on choice.
evidence: This is a critical assessment of existing literature based on methodological considerations.

claim: The right human frontal eye field (FEF) is a brain region often reported to be activated during the control of both eye movements and selective visual attention.
source: We employed transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) and targeted the right human frontal eye field (FEF) – a brain region often reported to be activated during the control of both eye movements and selective visual attention (Corbetta and Shulman, 2002; Hung et al., 2011; Juan and Muggleton, 2012; Marshall et al., 2015; Moore and Zirnsak, 2017; Schall, 2015)
evidence: This is supported by citations to neuroimaging and neurophysiology literature.

claim: Gaze has an amplifying effect on subjective values in the aDDM.
source: Our choice task capitalizes on an important feature of the aDDM, namely that gaze has an amplifying effect on subjective values and so has a stronger effect on decisions between high-value items than low-value items (Shevlin and Krajbich, 2021; Smith and Krajbich, 2019; Westbrook et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to aDDM literature and is a key theoretical prediction.

claim: Gaze has a stronger effect on decisions between high-value items than low-value items.
source: Our choice task capitalizes on an important feature of the aDDM, namely that gaze has an amplifying effect on subjective values and so has a stronger effect on decisions between high-value items than low-value items (Shevlin and Krajbich, 2021; Smith and Krajbich, 2019; Westbrook et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to aDDM literature and is a key theoretical prediction tested in the study.

claim: Forty-five subjects participated in the experiment.
source: Forty-five subjects participated in the experiment.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental sample size.

claim: Subjects rated 148 different food items on a scale from 0 to 10 based on how much they would like to eat the food.
source: First, subjects rated 148 different food items on a scale from 0 to 10 based on how much they would like to eat the food, or pressed the space bar for foods they did not want to eat (Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure, supported by reference to Figure 1A.

claim: Twenty-three subjects received inhibitory TMS over the right FEF.
source: After the rating task, subjects received inhibitory TMS over the right FEF (n = 23) or control TMS over the vertex (n = 22) (Figure 1D).
evidence: This describes the experimental groups and sample sizes.

claim: Twenty-two subjects received control TMS over the vertex.
source: After the rating task, subjects received inhibitory TMS over the right FEF (n = 23) or control TMS over the vertex (n = 22) (Figure 1D).
evidence: This describes the control group and sample size.

claim: Subjects made 180 decisions between pairs of positively rated food items immediately after the TMS procedure.
source: In the second task, immediately after the TMS procedure, subjects made 180 decisions between pairs of positively rated food items (Figure 1B).
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure and timing.

claim: The choice task had two conditions differing with respect to overall value (OV = left item value + right item value).
source: The task had two conditions, differing with respect to overall value (OV = left item value+ right item value).
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: In the high OV condition, subjects chose between two very appetitive (highly rated) foods.
source: In the high OV condition, subjects had to choose between two very appetitive (highly rated) foods, while decisions in the low OV condition only involved slightly appetitive (low rated) options (Figure 1C).
evidence: This describes the experimental conditions.

claim: In the low OV condition, decisions only involved slightly appetitive (low rated) options.
source: In the high OV condition, subjects had to choose between two very appetitive (highly rated) foods, while decisions in the low OV condition only involved slightly appetitive (low rated) options (Figure 1C).
evidence: This describes the experimental conditions.

claim: Subjects' gaze was recorded at 250 Hz with an EyeLink-1000 during the binary choice task.
source: During the binary choice task, we recorded subjects' gaze at 250 Hz with an EyeLink-1000 (http://www.sr-research.com/).
evidence: This describes the measurement method for gaze tracking.

claim: In the standard DDM, decision makers accumulate noisy evidence for options until the net evidence reaches a predefined boundary.
source: In the standard DDM, decision makers accumulate noisy evidence for the options until the net evidence reaches a predefined boundary.
evidence: This describes the standard DDM framework from established literature.

claim: In a value-based DDM, the rate of evidence accumulation (drift rate) reflects the difference in subjective values of the options.
source: In a value-based DDM, the rate of evidence accumulation ('drift rate') thus reflects the difference in subjective values of the options.
evidence: This describes the value-based extension of the DDM from established literature.

claim: The aDDM extends the standard DDM by allowing the drift rate to change within a trial based on which option is fixated.
source: The aDDM extends this model by allowing the drift rate to change within a trial, based on which option is fixated.
evidence: This describes the key feature of the aDDM framework.

claim: The aDDM assumes that gaze amplifies the value of the fixated (relative to non-fixated) option.
source: In particular, the model assumes that gaze amplifies the value of the fixated (relative to non-fixated) option, shifting the drift rate toward that choice option and increasing the likelihood that it is chosen.
evidence: This describes a key assumption of the aDDM framework.

claim: Because of the amplifying (multiplicative) mechanism in the aDDM, gaze has a stronger effect on the drift rate for high-value options.
source: Because of this amplifying (multiplicative) mechanism in the model, gaze has a stronger effect on the drift rate for high-value options, leading to shorter reaction times (RTs) and a larger effect of dwell time on choice probability (Shevlin and Krajbich, 2021; Smith and Krajbich, 2019; Westbrook et al., 2020; Figure 2).
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction of the aDDM supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 2.

claim: The amplifying mechanism in the aDDM leads to shorter reaction times for high-value options.
source: Because of this amplifying (multiplicative) mechanism in the model, gaze has a stronger effect on the drift rate for high-value options, leading to shorter reaction times (RTs) and a larger effect of dwell time on choice probability (Shevlin and Krajbich, 2021; Smith and Krajbich, 2019; Westbrook et al., 2020; Figure 2).
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction of the aDDM supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 2.

claim: The amplifying mechanism in the aDDM leads to a larger effect of dwell time on choice probability for high-value options.
source: Because of this amplifying (multiplicative) mechanism in the model, gaze has a stronger effect on the drift rate for high-value options, leading to shorter reaction times (RTs) and a larger effect of dwell time on choice probability (Shevlin and Krajbich, 2021; Smith and Krajbich, 2019; Westbrook et al., 2020; Figure 2).
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction of the aDDM supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 2.

claim: Subjects had a strong tendency to look first at the left food item (69.3%, 95% CI = [62.4%, 76.1%], p = 10–6).
source: Our subjects had a strong tendency to look first at the left food item (69.3%, 95% CI = [62.4%, 76.1%], p = 10–6) (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data with statistical support.

claim: A subject's first gaze was no more likely than chance to go to the higher-rated item (50.2%, CI = [49.0%, 51.3%], p = 0.78).
source: Consistent with prior work (Krajbich et al., 2010), a subject's first gaze was no more likely than chance to go to the higher-rated item (50.2%, CI = [49.0%, 51.3%], p = 0.78).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data, consistent with prior literature.

claim: FEF TMS did not induce any observable changes in dwell times relative to vertex TMS.
source: In the regression analyses, we found no hint of any main TMS effects or interaction effects (all p > 0.2) (see Materials and methods). Therefore, we conclude that FEF TMS did not induce any observable changes in dwell times relative to vertex TMS.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on regression analyses of the experimental data.

claim: The difference in dwell-time effects between low and high OV was eliminated in the FEF-TMS subjects.
source: In fact, the difference in dwell-time effects between low and high OV was eliminated in the FEF-TMS subjects, suggestive of a disruption of the multiplicative effect of gaze on value processing of the fixated option (Figure 4A, see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is an inference from the regression results, illustrated in Figure 4A.

claim: K-S tests revealed no difference between stimulation groups for low-OV trials (D = 0.022, p = 0.71).
source: K-S tests revealed no difference between stimulation groups for low-OV trials (D = 0.022, p = 0.71)
evidence: This is a finding from Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests of RT distributions.

claim: K-S tests revealed a significant difference between stimulation groups for high-OV trials (D = 0.064, p = 0.005).
source: but a significant difference for high-OV trials (D = 0.064, p = 0.005) (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a finding from Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests of RT distributions, illustrated in Figure 4B.

claim: K-S tests revealed significant differences between high- and low-OV trials in both groups.
source: They also revealed significant differences between high- and low-OV trials in both groups, though the difference was numerically larger for the vertex group (D = 0.097, p = 10–8) than for the FEF group (D = 0.091, p = 10–7).
evidence: This is a finding from Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests of RT distributions.

claim: The difference in RT distributions between high- and low-OV trials was numerically larger for the vertex group (D = 0.097, p = 10–8) than for the FEF group (D = 0.091, p = 10–7).
source: They also revealed significant differences between high- and low-OV trials in both groups, though the difference was numerically larger for the vertex group (D = 0.097, p = 10–8) than for the FEF group (D = 0.091, p = 10–7).
evidence: This is a finding from Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests of RT distributions.

claim: There was no difference in threshold separation between the FEF and vertex groups at the group level (aFEF = 2.67, [2.42, 2.85]; avertex = 2.63, [2.42, 2.94]; mean difference = 0.042, [–0.337, 0.434], p(avertex< aFEF) = 0.60).
source: Looking first at threshold separation, we found no difference between the groups, either in the group-level parameter distributions (aFEF = 2.67, [2.42, 2.85]; avertex = 2.63, [2.42, 2.94]; mean difference = 0.042, [–0.337, 0.434], p(avertex< aFEF) = 0.60)
evidence: This is a finding from hierarchical diffusion model fitting using HDDM.

claim: There was no difference in threshold separation between the FEF and vertex groups at the subject level (t(40.3) = 0.29, p = 0.78).
source: or in the subject-level parameter estimates (t(40.3) = 0.29, p = 0.78).
evidence: This is a finding from hierarchical diffusion model fitting using HDDM.

claim: There was no change in response caution between the two groups.
source: This clearly indicates that there was no change in response caution between the two groups.
evidence: This is an inference from the threshold separation parameter estimates.

claim: There was no difference in non-decision-time parameter between the groups at the group level (TerFEF = 694 ms, [633, 762]; Tervertex = 666 ms, [609, 728]; mean difference = 0.029, [–0.073, 0.126], p(Tervertex< TerFEF) = 0.74).
source: Looking next at the non-decision-time parameter, we again found no difference between the groups, either in the group-level parameter distributions (TerFEF = 694 ms, [633, 762]; Tervertex = 666 ms, [609, 728]; mean difference = 0.029, [–0.073, 0.126], p(Tervertex< TerFEF) = 0.74)
evidence: This is a finding from hierarchical diffusion model fitting using HDDM.

claim: There was no difference in non-decision-time parameter between the groups at the subject level (t(42.8) = 0.72, p = 0.47).
source: or in the subject-level parameter estimates (t(42.8) = 0.72, p = 0.47).
evidence: This is a finding from hierarchical diffusion model fitting using HDDM.

claim: There was no change in general RT components that are separate from the decision process between the two groups.
source: This indicates that there was also no change in general RT components that are separate from the decision process.
evidence: This is an inference from the non-decision-time parameter estimates.

claim: Additive effects of gaze direction did not differ between the groups at the subject level (t(40.1) = 0.86, p = 0.40).
source: or in the subject-level parameter estimates (t(40.1) = 0.86, p = 0.40).
evidence: This is a finding from hierarchical diffusion model fitting using HDDM.

claim: The estimated θ was lower for the vertex group (θ = 0.744) than for the FEF group (θ = 0.902), marginally at the group level (mean difference = 0.160 [–0.141, 0.468], p(θvertex< θFEF) = 0.89).
source: Comparing the two groups on the θ estimates, we found that the estimated θ was lower for the vertex group (θ = 0.744) than for the FEF group (θ = 0.902), marginally at the group level (mean difference = 0.160 [–0.141, 0.468], p(θvertex< θFEF) = 0.89)
evidence: This is a key finding from hierarchical diffusion model fitting using HDDM.

claim: The estimated θ was lower for the vertex group than for the FEF group, significantly at the subject level (t(42.9) = 2.85, p = 0.007).
source: and significantly at the subject level (t(42.9) = 2.85, p = 0.007).
evidence: This is a key finding from hierarchical diffusion model fitting using HDDM.

claim: The effects on choice behavior induced by TMS on the right FEF were specifically due to the multiplicative aDDM effects, and not due to changes in response caution, non-decision-time, or additive gaze effects.
source: This suggests that the effects on choice behavior induced by TMS on the right FEF were specifically due to the multiplicative aDDM effects, and not due to changes in response caution, non-decision-time, or additive gaze effects.
evidence: This is an inference from the pattern of diffusion model parameter estimates.

claim: In the FEF group, there was evidence for a starting-point bias to the left (z = 0.506, [0.493, 0.519]) compared to the vertex group (z = 0.491, [0.477, 0.506]) at the group level (mean difference = 0.014 [–0.007, 0.037], p(θvertex< θFEF) = 0.93).
source: In the FEF group, we found evidence for a starting-point bias to the left but for a drift-rate bias to the right, relative to the vertex group. The starting point in the FEF group (z = 0.506, [0.493, 0.519]) was greater than in the vertex group (z = 0.491, [0.477, 0.506]) at the group level (mean difference = 0.014 [–0.007, 0.037], p(θvertex< θFEF) = 0.93)
evidence: This is a finding from hierarchical diffusion model fitting using HDDM.

claim: In the FEF group, there was a starting-point bias to the left at the subject level (t(29.3) = 3.64, p = 0.001).
source: and at the subject level (t(29.3) = 3.64, p = 0.001).
evidence: This is a finding from hierarchical diffusion model fitting using HDDM.

claim: The drift-rate intercept in the FEF group was lower than in the vertex group at the subject level (t(36.3) = –3.44, p = 0.001).
source: and at the subject level (t(36.3) = –3.44, p = 0.001).
evidence: This is a finding from hierarchical diffusion model fitting using HDDM.

claim: The starting-point and drift-rate biases in the FEF group do not have a net biasing effect on behavior because they are of opposite direction.
source: Please note that because these effects are of opposite direction, they do not have a net biasing effect on behavior.
evidence: This is an inference from the pattern of parameter estimates.

claim: FEF TMS reduces the effect of gaze on choice in high-value trials even when the observed gaze patterns and possible complex spatial biases are accounted for.
source: In sum, the results that we have presented demonstrate that FEF TMS reduces the effect of gaze on choice even when the observed gaze patterns and possible complex spatial biases are accounted for.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the modeling results.

claim: FEF TMS has effects on value discounting during choice that are independent of any effects the stimulation may have on gaze patterns or spatial biases themselves.
source: Thus, FEF TMS has effects on value discounting during choice that are independent of any effects the stimulation may have on gaze patterns or spatial biases themselves.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the modeling results that accounts for potential confounds.

claim: The findings provide a neural validation for a central assumption in the aDDM, namely that overt attention amplifies the subjective values of the items.
source: Our results provide a neural validation for a central assumption in the aDDM, namely that overt attention amplifies the subjective values of the items, leading to larger effects on choice for higher-valued items (Smith and Krajbich, 2019).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results in the context of the aDDM framework.

claim: FEF stimulation affected choices and RTs in high-value but not low-value trials.
source: By showing that FEF stimulation affected choices and RTs in high-value but not low-value trials, we confirmed a role for right FEF in attention-based value modulation during choice, and further validated the multiplicative nature of the aDDM (Westbrook et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a summary of the key experimental findings.

claim: The right FEF plays a role in attention-based value modulation during choice.
source: By showing that FEF stimulation affected choices and RTs in high-value but not low-value trials, we confirmed a role for right FEF in attention-based value modulation during choice, and further validated the multiplicative nature of the aDDM (Westbrook et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the experimental findings.

claim: The findings validate the multiplicative nature of the aDDM.
source: By showing that FEF stimulation affected choices and RTs in high-value but not low-value trials, we confirmed a role for right FEF in attention-based value modulation during choice, and further validated the multiplicative nature of the aDDM (Westbrook et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the experimental findings in the context of the aDDM framework.

claim: DDM-like neural mechanisms underlie value-based choice.
source: More generally, our results build on a literature documenting the DDM-like neural mechanisms underlying value-based choice.
evidence: This is a statement about existing literature that the current results build upon.

claim: EEG, fMRI, and their combination have been used to identify neural signatures of evidence accumulation in structures such as the dorsal/posterior medial prefrontal cortex, dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, and intraparietal sulci.
source: These papers have used EEG (Polanía et al., 2014), fMRI (Basten et al., 2010; Gluth et al., 2012; Hare et al., 2011; Lim et al., 2011; Rodriguez et al., 2015), and their combination (Pisauro et al., 2017), to identify neural signatures of evidence accumulation in structures such as the dorsal/posterior medial prefrontal cortex, dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, and intraparietal sulci.
evidence: This is a summary of existing literature with citations.

claim: The right FEF may play a critical role in contributing to integration activity in brain regions involved in value-based choice, through implementing a multiplicative value-discounting effect linked to the focus of overt attention.
source: Our results suggest that the right FEF may play a critical role in contributing to the resulting integration activity in this set of regions, through implementing a multiplicative value-discounting effect linked to the focus of overt attention.
evidence: This is an interpretation and speculation based on the experimental results.

claim: Relative to unattended visual stimuli, perceptual sensitivity is enhanced for attended elements of the visual scene.
source: As for perception – where mainly covert rather than overt attention has been studied – previous psychophysical studies have shown that, relative to unattended visual stimuli, perceptual sensitivity is enhanced for attended elements of the visual scene (Barbot et al., 2011; Herrmann et al., 2010; Montagna et al., 2009; Pestilli et al., 2007; Pestilli and Carrasco, 2005).
evidence: This is a summary of existing literature on perceptual attention with citations.

claim: Attended visual stimuli may have stronger neural representations than unattended ones.
source: These investigations suggest that attended visual stimuli may have stronger neural representations than unattended ones, and this view has been supported by neurophysiological reports in humans (Kastner et al., 1998; Liu et al., 2005; O'Craven et al., 1997) and non-human primates (Connor et al., 1997; Martínez-Trujillo and Treue, 2002; Reynolds et al., 2000; Reynolds and Desimone, 2003).
evidence: This is a summary of existing literature with citations to neurophysiological studies.

claim: Neuronal populations that code for covertly attended locations of the visual scene display enhanced activity, relative to neurons representing unattended locations.
source: More precisely, these investigations have shown that neuronal populations that code for covertly attended locations of the visual scene display enhanced activity, relative to neurons representing unattended locations.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from neurophysiological literature.

claim: The FEF is a possible source of attention-dependent modulations in visual areas.
source: Importantly, the FEF is a possible source of these attention-dependent modulations: Investigations combining brain stimulation with neuroimaging techniques have shown that modulations of neuronal activity in the FEF induce top-down modulatory effects on both behavior and neuronal activity in early visual areas that resemble effects of attention (Moore and Armstrong, 2003; Moore and Fallah, 2004; Ruff et al., 2006; Silvanto et al., 2006; Taylor et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a summary of existing literature with citations to brain stimulation studies.

claim: Attention-dependent behavioral effects are due to a boost in synchronization between FEF and V4 at the gamma-band frequency.
source: Additionally, it has been suggested that attention-dependent behavioral effects are due to a boost in synchronization between FEF and V4 at the gamma-band frequency (Gregoriou et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a summary of a specific finding from the literature with citation.

claim: Value representations are found in a large network of brain areas including the ventromedial prefrontal cortex, orbitofrontal cortex, ventral striatum, and the posterior parietal cortex.
source: Extensive research indicates that such value representations are found in a large network of brain areas including the ventromedial prefrontal cortex, orbitofrontal cortex, ventral striatum, and the posterior parietal cortex (Bartra et al., 2013; Boorman et al., 2009; Clithero and Rangel, 2014; Cromwell and Schultz, 2003; Kahnt et al., 2014; Knutson et al., 2001; Padoa-Schioppa and Assad, 2006; Plassmann et al., 2007; Platt and Glimcher, 1999).
evidence: This is a summary of existing literature on value representations with citations.

claim: Value-related BOLD signals are increased when attention is directed to the value (rather than other aspects) of objects.
source: Moreover, these value-related BOLD signals are increased when attention is directed to the value (rather than other aspects) of objects (Grueschow et al., 2015; Grabenhorst and Rolls, 2008), or when participants attend to specific value-relevant aspects of a given stimulus (Lim et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a summary of existing literature with citations.

claim: Attending to the value of items leads to increases in fronto-posterior synchronization in the gamma frequency.
source: Interestingly, in another analogy to the perceptual domain, attending to the value of items leads to increases in fronto-posterior synchronization in the gamma frequency (Polanía et al., 2014)
evidence: This is a summary of a specific finding from the literature with citation.

claim: Decreasing the degree of fronto-posterior gamma coherence by brain stimulation leads to inaccurate value-based choices.
source: and decreasing the degree of this coherence by brain stimulation leads to inaccurate value-based choices (Polanía et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a summary of a specific finding from the literature with citation.

claim: Many of the attentional effects of the FEF in the human brain appear to be lateralized to the right FEF.
source: Moreover, given that many of the attentional effects of the FEF in the human brain appear to be lateralized to the right FEF (Ruff et al., 2009; Vernet et al., 2014)
evidence: This is a summary of existing literature with citations.

claim: The findings demonstrate the relevance of the FEF for gaze-dependent modulations of value-based decision processes.
source: Taken together, our findings demonstrate the relevance of the FEF for gaze-dependent modulations of value-based decision processes
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the experimental findings.

claim: Forty-five right-handed subjects (20 females, mean age ± SD = 23.14 ± 2.39) without a history of implanted metal objects, seizures, or any other neurological or psychiatric disease participated in the experiment.
